answers.justification: C2 shows pay at the 54th–61st percentile like the rest of the firm, a rival gap of £3–5k rather than £15k, and 6 of 8 known leavers taking equal or lower pay, mostly moving in-house or to the regulator; E4/C9 fair-pay scores of about 3.0 are middling.

Resignations cluster under Faulk (C1: 8 of 11 vs 1 of 13) and E4/C6 contain complaints about him, but Faulk supervises every Kestrel associate and no other matter (C1), so supervision cannot be separated from Kestrel workload (C4, C14); C6 says the reasons were mixed.

Kestrel assignment goes with resignation (C1) and with very high hours and weekend work (C4, E4), but the matter is fully confounded with Faulk's supervision (C1, C6), so workload is live but not shown to be the driver.

The target rise applied to every group (C8, E2), yet other groups' attrition held flat (E2), non-Kestrel associates in the group averaged 1,940 hours (C4), and only 1 of 13 non-Kestrel associates left (C1).
Market attrition was 14% and slightly falling (C11) and other groups were flat (E2), while the group hit 37.5% with 8 of 9 leavers from one matter team (C1), which rules out ordinary mobility.
Faulk's supervision coincides with 8 of 9 resignations (C1), but it is perfectly collinear with Kestrel workload (C1, C4), so causation cannot be attributed to supervision.

Kestrel assignment strongly predicts resignation (C1) and comes with extreme hours (C4), but it is confounded with Faulk's supervision (C1) and possibly with selection of low-utilisation associates (C1 staffing note), so causation is not isolated.

There is no meaningful pay gap (C2: market-level salaries, a £3–5k rival band), most leavers took equal or lower pay (C2), and they went in-house or to the regulator rather than to better-paying firms.
The same target change (C8) left other groups' attrition unchanged (E2), and non-Kestrel associates in the group rarely left (C1) even though their hours were near the firm norm (C4).

Separating supervision from workload is the key unresolved question, because they are confounded (C1, C6) and existing exit data is uninformative (C3, C15); the interviews are cheap and quick (E5: £9k, three weeks, four leavers already willing).
It targets a cause the evidence contradicts (C2), costs £228k (E5), and closing the review would hide the Kestrel-specific driver (C1, C4).

It would be right if H2 were confirmed, but supervision is confounded with workload (C1, C6), Faulk is the named supervising partner on the engagement (C12), and the client values the current team (C10).

It would be right if H3 were confirmed, but workload is not separated from supervision (C1), the £160k must be absorbed by the firm (E5, C12), and the review phase ends in December 2026 anyway (E3, C12).
The current attrition data lacks matter and supervisor fields (E2, C3), so adding them is a cheap and sensible fix, but it does not settle the present question in time.
The leading substantive actions (A3 or A4) depend on which of the two fully confounded causes (C1) is operating, and nothing in the catalogue separates them (C6, C9, C3).

ambiguousItems: I3: H3 could defensibly be 'supported' because hours are extreme (C4) and E4 comments focus on workload, though it is confounded with H2
I14: A5 could be 'preferred' as low-cost monitoring alongside A1
I13: A4 could be 'acceptable', since relieving workload helps whichever cause is operating, though the firm-funded cost argues against it
I7: R2 could be read as stronger than association-only, given the dose-like hours difference in C4
caseProblems: E4 says 20 associates were in the group in July 2026, but the case gives 24 opening associates, 7 resignations by June and 4 lateral hires, which implies about 21 unless a lateral joined after July; the timing is unspecified.
C1 records 8 of 11 Kestrel associates resigning but says nothing about backfilling, even though the planned complement was 9–11 through December 2026 (C12).
The C1 staffing note (Kestrel places filled from the associates with the lowest forward utilisation) introduces a possible selection confound that the candidate hypotheses never address.
C9 merges any band with fewer than five responses, so 15 responses across three reported bands means exactly five in each. This is plausible but a fragile anonymity setup.
Catalogue titles do not leak the answers, but C1 alone almost settles that the Kestrel/Faulk cluster is the driver.

rulings.explanation: The key's 'unknown' holds. Under the task's definition, 'supported' needs the evidence to favour H3 over its rivals, and H2 is a live rival that the evidence treats the same way. C1 shows complete overlap: all 11 Kestrel associates were under Faulk, Faulk supervised no one else, and no associate logged Kestrel time under another partner. C4 confirms extreme hours, but it also says no other team in the group averaged above 2,050 hours, so there is no heavy-hours team without Faulk to compare against. E4 does not favour workload either. Workload scores 2.3 against 3.4 and respect scores 2.8 against 3.9, the same gap, and the free text includes both 'months of weekends' and 'drafts come back after midnight… humiliating'. C6 gives split reasons ('the hours', 'Dorian', 'all of it'). C5 and C14 come from interested parties. C1's note that Kestrel was staffed from the associates with the lowest forward utilisation adds a selection rival. H1, H4 and H5 are ruled out, but that does not lift H3 above H2. So 'unknown' is the only defensible answer.

The key's 'acceptable' holds. A5 is reasonable because it fixes a real reporting gap: E2 records neither matter nor partner. But 'preferred' means among the best next actions for the decision in front of the committee, and A5 cannot inform that decision. Monthly tracking only produces data going forward. Because Faulk is the only partner on Kestrel and C12 names him for both phases, new matter and partner fields would still record the two exposures together. They could not separate supervision from workload on any timescale relevant to the decision. A1 can separate them within three weeks for about £9k. Running A5 alongside A1 is sensible, but that makes it a reasonable complement ('acceptable'), not one of the best actions.
rulings.fix: None needed. Optionally, add one clause to A5's rationale, or a line to C12, noting that Faulk will remain the only partner on Kestrel, so the new fields would still record the two exposures together. That makes the 'cannot discriminate' point explicit.

rulings.explanation: The key's 'premature' holds. The flag argues that relieving workload would help whichever cause is operating, but the evidence does not back that. Contract reviewers would take over first-level review only. Kestrel associates would stay under Faulk, and the supervision behaviour described in E4 and C5 (late-night corrections copied to the whole team) would continue. So A4 depends on H3, which is unestablished and confounded with H2. That matches the definition of 'premature': it could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed. The other factors also count against 'acceptable'. It costs about £160k, firm-funded because the client will not pay (E5, C12), against £9k for the interviews that would settle the question in three weeks. The review phase ends in December 2026, and the January 2027 phase change would confound any read of whether it worked. Faulk's remark in C14 that he is keeping people late because of short staffing hints that workload drives some of the supervision behaviour. But that account comes from an interested party and does not establish that A4 would fix a supervision problem.
rulings.fix: None needed. Optionally, state in E5 or C12 that contract reviewers would not change who supervises associates' drafting and corrections. That would close off the 'helps either way' reading completely.

rulings.explanation: The key's 'association-only' holds. C4 does not give a dose-response. It compares group-level averages (Kestrel 2,270 hours against 1,940 for the rest of the group), not individual hours against individual resignations. It also states that no other team in the group averaged above 2,050 hours, so there is no high-hours team without Faulk to show workload acting alone. Under the task's definition, 'causal' requires the main rival to be ruled out, and here it is not. The rival exposure (Faulk's supervision) covers exactly the same associates (C1), and staffing by low utilisation is a further selection rival. Strong covariation plus a plausible mechanism, with the confounder still in place, is association only.
